summary: 11a opens by identifying the tanna behind the baraita that all Temple gates lacked a mezuza except Nicanor Gate, concluding even R. Yehuda could hold it since gate and chamber form one combined rabbinic decree. The Gemara then broadens to general mezuza law: city gates and all four types of public gates require a mezuza, but Machoza's city gates lacked one due to the danger of checking - public mezuzot are checked only twice per jubilee, and a checker could be fined 1000 zuz. The rest of the daf debates whether storehouses for hay, cattle, wood, and general storage require a mezuza: Rav Kahana teaches before Rav Yehuda that all four are exempt because 'nashim ne'otot bahen' (women make use of them), a phrase the two amora'im read differently (bathe vs. adorn themselves) as each reading is challenged by a conflicting baraita, until Rav Kahana concludes the whole matter - both the meaning of the phrase and the status of standard storehouses - is a tannaitic dispute. A further baraita listing bathroom, tannery, bathhouse, and mikveh as always exempt is read by each amora according to his own reasoning, and the daf closes mid-sentence on a baraita that appears to obligate even barns, hay-storehouses, and wine/oil storehouses, a difficulty resolved only on 11b.

display.title: The tanna behind the Temple-gates baraita
display.oneLine: The Gemara identifies whose view the baraita (all Temple gates lack mezuza except Nicanor Gate) reflects, and shows even R. Yehuda can hold it.
display.shortSummary: A baraita states all Temple gates lacked a mezuza except the Nicanor Gate, which had one because caretakers resided in its chambers. The Gemara asks whose view this is. The concern: if the baraita reflects R. Yehuda's position, does it create a gezeira ligzeira - a rabbinic decree protecting a rabbinic decree (Parhedrin chamber decree + Temple-gates decree)? The Gemara resolves this by treating the gate and the Parhedrin chamber as one unified decree, not two separate ones layered on each other.
display.whats: The Gemara identifies whose view the Temple-gates baraita reflects. The challenge: if it is R. Yehuda's view, then the Parhedrin chamber already has a mezuza only by rabbinic decree - can we pile a second rabbinic decree on top of that (the Temple-gates decree)? The Gemara resolves: the gate and chamber are treated as one unified decree, avoiding the gezeira ligzeira problem.
display.hint: The rule against gezeira ligzeira (a decree to protect a decree) is a significant principle limiting rabbinic legislation - so how does the Gemara let this baraita hold even for R. Yehuda?

learning.learnerQuestion: Why does it matter which tanna authored the Temple-gates baraita? And what is the gezeira ligzeira problem?
learning.coreTension: If R. Yehuda holds the Parhedrin mezuza is only rabbinic, then requiring mezuza for the Nicanor Gate (to protect people from thinking the Parhedrin chamber lacks one) would be a decree protecting a decree - normally forbidden. The Gemara needs to show this is not actually gezeira ligzeira.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara collapses the gate and chamber into one combined rabbinic decree rather than treating them as two separate decrees in sequence. This avoids the prohibition on stacking rabbinic decrees.
learning.resolution: The Temple-gates baraita can reflect R. Yehuda's position because gate and chamber form a single unit - the decree applies to the whole structure, not to each part separately.

takeaway.text: Rabbinic decrees that apply to connected structures can be treated as one ruling rather than two stacked decrees. The prohibition on gezeira ligzeira applies to distinct independent decrees, not to one ruling that covers a connected structure.

reasoningPattern.notes: The Gemara avoids the gezeira ligzeira problem by recharacterizing the two rulings (gate + chamber) as one. This is a standard Talmudic move: when a logical problem threatens a ruling, reframe the ruling's scope.

learning.ahaMoment: The Nicanor Gate specifically had a mezuza (unlike all other Temple gates) because a caretaker lived in its chambers. The gate requirement follows the residence - once someone genuinely lives there, the whole entrance requires a mezuza.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may not understand why gezeira ligzeira is forbidden. The concern is that stacking rabbinic decrees leads to ever-expanding obligations that were never intended by Torah law. The Sages limited this by prohibiting decrees whose sole purpose is to protect another decree.
learning.memoryAnchor: All Temple gates: no mezuza. Nicanor Gate: mezuza - because someone lived there. R. Yehuda can hold this without gezeira ligzeira because gate and chamber are one unit, not two decrees stacked.

argumentFlow.label: Who authored the Temple-gates baraita?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: A baraita teaches all Temple gates lacked a mezuza except Nicanor Gate (where caretakers resided). The Gemara asks: whose position does this reflect?

argumentFlow.label: Even R. Yehuda - gate and chamber are one decree
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Even R. Yehuda can hold this view, because the decree applies to the gate and chamber as a unified structure. There is no gezeira ligzeira problem when a single decree covers connected elements.

sourceRefs.note: Resolution: unified decree avoids the stacking problem

misconceptions.misconception: The Nicanor Gate had a mezuza because it was the most important gate.
misconceptions.correction: It had a mezuza because people (caretakers) lived in the chambers attached to it, not because of the gate's architectural or ritual prominence.

quizSeeds.answer: Because caretakers (gabba'im) resided in the chambers attached to the Nicanor Gate, making those chambers genuine residences that required a mezuza.

quizSeeds.question: Why does the Temple-gates decree not constitute a gezeira ligzeira for R. Yehuda?
quizSeeds.answer: Because the gate and the Parhedrin chamber are treated as one unified structure subject to one decree, not two separate rabbinic decrees stacked on each other.

display.title: Which gates require a mezuza - and the danger of checking
display.oneLine: City gates and all four types of public gates require a mezuza, but Machoza's gates lacked one because checking a mezuza risked a 1000-zuz fine.
display.shortSummary: The Gemara establishes that city gates require a mezuza. It then asks why Machoza (a major Jewish city) had no mezuzot on its city gates. Rav Safra says the gates were structural reinforcements built into the wall, not real gates. Abaye challenges: then the fortified structure itself should require a mezuza. The real answer is danger: public mezuzot are checked only twice per jubilee (50 years), and Rav Yehuda relates that a certain Artavan who was checking mezuzot in the upper market of Tzippori was caught by an official and fined 1000 zuz. The Gemara asks: doesn't R. Elazar say agents of a mitzva are not harmed? It answers that this protection does not apply where the danger is fixed and known in advance, proving the point from the verse where Samuel feared Saul would kill him if he went to anoint David - an unrelated proof text about fixed danger, not a mezuza-checking incident.
display.whats: Two questions about city-gate mezuzot. First: why did Machoza's city gates lack mezuzot? Rav Safra's structural answer is rejected by Abaye. The real reason is danger: Rav Yehuda reports that Artavan was fined 1000 zuz by an official after checking mezuzot in Tzippori's upper market. The Gemara objects that agents of a mitzva are not harmed, and answers that this protection has an exception when the danger is fixed and predictable - proven from the verse where Samuel, told to anoint David, feared Saul would kill him if he found out.
display.hint: The principle 'shluchei mitzva einan nizzokin' (agents of a mitzva are not harmed) has a crucial exception - so how could Artavan still be fined 1000 zuz for checking a mezuza?

learning.learnerQuestion: If agents of a mitzva are divinely protected, why would checking a mezuza carry any real risk?
learning.coreTension: The general principle protects mitzva agents from harm, but Artavan was fined 1000 zuz for checking a mezuza in Tzippori. The exception for 'fixed and predictable danger' explains why divine protection did not shield him.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara distinguishes between unpredictable danger (covered by mitzva-agent protection) and danger that is fixed and known in advance (not covered), then proves the exception from Samuel's own words when told to anoint David.
learning.resolution: Machoza's gates lacked mezuzot because the danger of checking was real and predictable: an official could fine the checker 1000 zuz, as happened to Artavan in Tzippori. This is the kind of fixed danger that mitzva-agent protection does not eliminate.

takeaway.text: Mitzva-agent protection is not a blanket exemption from all harm. When danger is specific, predictable, and human in origin (like a legal fine), one should not rely on divine protection and may legitimately avoid the risky action.

reasoningPattern.notes: The exception (fixed predictable danger) is as important as the rule. Knowing when a principle does not apply is as essential as knowing the principle itself.

learning.ahaMoment: The proof for the exception comes from Samuel's own fear when God told him to anoint David: 'How can I go? Saul will hear and kill me.' Samuel never checked a mezuza - the Gemara cites him only to show that even a prophet recognizes fixed, known danger as different from ordinary risk.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may conflate Artavan, who actually checked mezuzot and was fined, with Samuel, who is quoted only as a scriptural proof text about fixed danger. The Gemara actually says public mezuzot are required - the Machoza case is an exception justified by specific predictable danger, not a general exemption for public gates.
learning.memoryAnchor: City gates need mezuza. Machoza: no mezuza. Why? Artavan was fined 1000 zuz for checking a mezuza in Tzippori. Mitzva-agent protection does not cover predictable human penalties - proven from Samuel's fear of Saul, a separate proof text, not a mezuza story.

argumentFlow.label: City gates require a mezuza
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara establishes that city gates and all four types of public gates require a mezuza. This raises the question about Machoza.

sourceRefs.note: General rule: city gates require mezuza

argumentFlow.label: Why did Machoza's city gates lack mezuzot?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rav Safra's answer: the Machoza gates were structural reinforcements built into the city wall, not real gates. Abaye rejects this: then the whole fortified structure should require a mezuza.

sourceRefs.note: Rav Safra's answer rejected by Abaye

argumentFlow.label: Real reason: danger from the checking fine
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The real reason Machoza's gates lacked mezuzot: public mezuzot are only checked twice per jubilee. Rav Yehuda relates that a certain Artavan, while checking mezuzot in the upper market of Tzippori, was caught by an official who fined him 1000 zuz.

argumentFlow.label: Proof from Samuel: fixed danger is an exception to mitzva-agent protection
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara objects: didn't R. Elazar say agents of a mitzva are not harmed - so how was Artavan fined? It answers that this protection does not apply where the danger is fixed and known in advance, proving this from Samuel's words when told to anoint David: 'How can I go? Saul will hear and kill me.' Samuel's fear of a known, predictable threat is the proof text - he is not described as checking or declining to check a mezuza.

misconceptions.misconception: Machoza's gates lacked mezuzot because they were not real gates or not obligated.
misconceptions.correction: City gates are obligated. Machoza's gates lacked mezuzot because of the specific danger of the checking fine - a predictable legal risk that mitzva-agent protection does not cover.

misconceptions.misconception: Samuel checked (or refused to check) a mezuza and was fined or endangered for it.
misconceptions.correction: The mezuza-checking incident and 1000-zuz fine happened to Artavan in Tzippori's upper market. Samuel is quoted only for an unrelated verse - his fear that Saul would kill him if he went to anoint David - cited purely as scriptural proof that fixed, known danger is an exception to mitzva-agent protection.

quizSeeds.question: Why did Machoza's city gates lack mezuzot even though city gates generally require them?
quizSeeds.answer: Because checking public mezuzot carried a risk of a 1000-zuz fine if a defective mezuza was found, and since this danger was fixed and predictable, the protection for mitzva-agents did not apply.

quizSeeds.question: When does the principle 'shluchei mitzva einan nizzokin' NOT apply?
quizSeeds.answer: When the danger is fixed and predictable. Divine protection applies to unexpected supernatural danger, not to predictable human-imposed consequences like legal fines.

display.title: Storehouses and the mezuza dispute between Rav Kahana and Rav Yehuda
display.oneLine: Rav Kahana and Rav Yehuda dispute what 'nashim ne'otot bahen' (women make use of them) means for exempting hay, cattle, wood and general storehouses from mezuza, and the debate ends as a tannaitic dispute.
display.shortSummary: Rav Kahana teaches before Rav Yehuda that storehouses for hay, cattle, wood, and general storage are all exempt from mezuza because women 'ne'otot' there, first explained as bathing. Rav Yehuda objects from a baraita that a cattle barn is exempt unconditionally, so Rav Kahana reinterprets ne'otot as adorning themselves - but a different baraita obligates a barn where women adorn themselves. Rav Kahana concludes both the meaning of ne'otot and the status of a standard storehouse are unresolved tannaitic disputes. Each amora then reads a further baraita (bathroom, tannery, bathhouse, mikveh always exempt) according to his own position, before a final baraita seemingly obligating barns and wine/oil storehouses cuts off mid-sentence.
display.whats: The storehouse debate shows how a single ambiguous phrase - 'nashim ne'otot bahen' - can be read two ways (bathe vs. adorn) and how each reading is tested against a conflicting baraita until the amora concedes the underlying law itself is disputed among tanna'im, not just the phrase's meaning. Hay, cattle, wood, and general storehouses are treated as one group throughout; there is no obligated/exempt split among these four in either amora's position - the dispute is whether the group is exempt only when women use it a certain way, or exempt outright.
display.hint: Can you track both layers of disagreement—what 'ne'otot' means and whether a standard storehouse is obligated or exempt—and explain why Rav Kahana concludes that both questions are tannaitic disputes?

learning.learnerQuestion: Why does the meaning of one word - 'ne'otot' - decide whether a storehouse needs a mezuza?
learning.coreTension: A storehouse is exempt from mezuza only if it is not a genuine dwelling. 'Nashim ne'otot bahen' is the baraita's stated reason for exemption, but the word is ambiguous, and each proposed meaning is immediately contradicted by another baraita.
learning.coreMove: Rather than settle on one meaning of 'ne'otot,' Rav Kahana ultimately argues that both the meaning of the word and the status of an ordinary (unmarked) storehouse are themselves disputed among tanna'im - the contradictions are not errors to reconcile but evidence of a real halakhic disagreement.
learning.resolution: Left as a tannaitic dispute on this daf; the underlying question of standard storehouses continues on 11b, but this daf ends before stating its resolution.

takeaway.text: When a legal formula's key term is ambiguous and each reading collides with a separate baraita, the Gemara may conclude that the underlying halakha is a genuine tannaitic dispute rather than force a single resolution.

reasoningPattern.notes: Rav Yehuda repeatedly refutes Rav Kahana's stated reason for an exemption by citing a baraita that contradicts the current reading of 'ne'otot.' Rav Kahana responds each time by proposing a new reading, until the pattern itself becomes the answer: this is a dispute, not a definition to be nailed down.

learning.ahaMoment: The exemption is never about hay vs. wood vs. wine specifically - all four storehouse types travel together in every version of the baraita. The entire fight is over what 'ne'otot' means and whether that meaning extends to the ordinary, non-marked case.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume the four storehouse types (hay, cattle, wood, general storage) are being split into obligated and exempt subsets. They are not - in every reading, all four are grouped together, and the only variable is the interpretation of 'ne'otot' and the standard-use question.
learning.memoryAnchor: Ne'otot = bathe (round 1) -> refuted by cattle-barn baraita. Ne'otot = adorn (round 2) -> refuted by a barn-where-they-adorn baraita. Round 3: it's a tannaitic dispute, on both questions.

argumentFlow.label: Rav Kahana: hay, cattle, wood, storehouse - all exempt because women 'ne'otot' there = bathe
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Kahana
argumentFlow.text: Rav Kahana teaches before Rav Yehuda that storehouses for hay, cattle, wood, and general storage are all exempt from mezuza because women 'ne'otot' (make use of) them - explained as bathing there. Rav Yehuda objects: if the reason is bathing, a standard (non-bathing) storehouse should be obligated - but a baraita says a cattle barn is exempt unconditionally.

sourceRefs.note: Rav Kahana's baraita and Rav Yehuda's first challenge from the unconditional cattle-barn exemption

argumentFlow.label: Reinterpreting ne'otot as 'adorn themselves' - and a new contradiction
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara reinterprets: 'ne'otot' means women adorn themselves there, and the baraita teaches that even where women adorn themselves, the storehouse is exempt. Rav Kahana's revised reading is itself contradicted: a baraita states that a barn where women adorn themselves IS obligated in mezuza.

sourceRefs.note: Second reading of ne'otot and its own contradicting baraita

argumentFlow.label: Rav Kahana: it is a tannaitic dispute - on both questions
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Kahana
argumentFlow.text: Rav Kahana concludes that whether 'adorning' produces exemption is itself a dispute among tanna'im - and, by the same token, so is the status of a standard storehouse, since a baraita on the exclusion of 'your house' both exempts these storehouses and notes that some obligate them.

sourceRefs.note: Rav Kahana generalizes: both the adorning question and the standard-use question are tannaitic disputes

argumentFlow.label: A further baraita: bathroom, tannery, bathhouse, mikveh always exempt
argumentFlow.speaker: Baraita
argumentFlow.text: A baraita states that in truth, a bathroom, a tannery, a bathhouse, and an immersion-house, and any place of which women make use, are exempt from mezuza - a ruling that fits neither Rav Kahana's nor Rav Yehuda's position as stated, so each interprets it according to his own reasoning.

sourceRefs.note: The 'be'emet amru' baraita and the need for each amora to reconcile it with his own view

argumentFlow.label: Rav Kahana's and Rav Yehuda's respective readings of the be'emet amru baraita
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rav Kahana reads the baraita as: storehouses are exempt only in the standard case, with some who obligate the standard case; the bathroom/tannery/bathhouse/mikveh group is exempt because women bathe there, and both public and private bathhouses are included despite the private bathhouse having less filth. Rav Yehuda reads it as: storehouses are exempt even where women adorn themselves, with some who obligate the adorning case; but everyone agrees the standard case is exempt, and the bathroom/tannery/bathhouse/mikveh group is exempt because its filth is extensive.

sourceRefs.note: Rav Kahana's reconciliation, including the public-vs-private bathhouse distinction
Rav Yehuda's reconciliation begins at the end of the line and continues through line 48

argumentFlow.label: A baraita seemingly obligating barns and storehouses challenges Rav Yehuda - daf ends mid-sentence
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara challenges Rav Yehuda: does everyone really agree the standard storehouse is exempt? A baraita on 'your gates' lists gates of houses, courtyards, cities, and towns, and also a barn, chicken coops, a hay-storehouse, and wine and oil storehouses, as all obligated in mezuza. The Gemara begins to qualify this baraita but the daf cuts off mid-word; the resolution continues on 11b.

sourceRefs.note: The obligating baraita challenging Rav Yehuda

misconceptions.misconception: Hay and cattle storehouses are exempt while wood and wine storehouses are obligated, as if the four types split into two groups.
misconceptions.correction: All four storehouse types (hay, cattle, wood, general storage) are grouped together in every version of the baraita discussed on this daf. The dispute is not about which of the four types is obligated, but about what 'ne'otot' means and whether the standard (unmarked) case is exempt or obligated - a question left as an unresolved tannaitic dispute.

visualizableElements.item: Two successive readings of 'ne'otot' (bathe, then adorn), each defeated by a different baraita
The four storehouse types (hay, cattle, wood, general storage) moving together as one exempt group across every reading

quizSeeds.question: According to the baraita Rav Kahana first teaches, why are storehouses for hay, cattle, wood, and general storage exempt from mezuza?
quizSeeds.answer: Because 'nashim ne'otot bahen' (women make use of them) - first explained to mean that women bathe there, making it inappropriate to affix a mezuza.

quizSeeds.question: What is Rav Kahana's ultimate resolution to the repeated contradictions over the meaning of 'ne'otot'?
quizSeeds.answer: That both the meaning of 'ne'otot' and the status of a standard (unmarked) storehouse are themselves disputed among tanna'im, rather than a single settled halakha.

prerequisiteKnowledge: That mezuza requires a 'dwelling' - a space used for genuine human residential purposes
That an ambiguous term in a baraita can be reinterpreted when the current reading is contradicted by another source
Basic storehouse structure and use in Talmudic times

glossary.en: A decree to protect a decree - normally prohibited in rabbinic legislation. The Gemara avoids this problem for the Temple-gates ruling by treating gate and chamber as one unified structure subject to a single decree.

Agents performing a mitzva are not harmed. A general principle of divine protection, with a crucial exception: when danger is fixed and predictable (like a legal fine), one may not rely on this protection.

Storehouse or treasury. The Gemara debates whether storehouses for hay, cattle, wood, and general storage require a mezuza, turning on the meaning of 'nashim ne'otot bahen' and left as an unresolved tannaitic dispute.

rashiTranslations.en: 'All the gates' - the eastern gates of the Temple courtyard. 'The gates of provinces alike' - there is a province
surrounded by mountains and forests for several parasangs, which one can leave only by way of
gates, such as the land of Hagar. 'the abulei of Machoza' - the gates of a city named Machoza,
most of whose people were Israelites. 'to the akra of Kuvei' - a structure is built over them, called Kuvei,
and the gates beneath it are made like an arch, and a building
built upon arches is stronger. 'and the akra
of Kuvei itself' - on account of that building itself,
the gate should require a mezuza, since through that gate
one enters it. 'because of danger' - lest
the king say: you have performed sorcery on the gates of my city.
'is checked' - whether it rotted or was stolen.
'and of the public' - the gates of courtyards, provinces,
and towns. 'twice in a jubilee' - anything
that belongs to the public, one may not impose much trouble
over it, for if you impose, each person will
say: my fellows will do it. 'beArtavin' - the name of
the man; and some say it is after his craft.
'kasdor' - it is the name of an office, like 'sardiyot',
and he is an officer. 'where the harm is fixed' - the ruler's
pretexts are ever ready. 'how can I go' -
to anoint David, at the word of God. 'the house of
storehouses' - of wine, of oil, and of grain, and no
person dwells in it. 'what is ne'otot? Bathing' -
'ne'otot' is a term of benefit; and because it is a place of
disgrace, where they stand there naked, it is not
the honor of Heaven for a mezuza to be there. 'even though
the women adorn themselves' - there, with perfumes,
and it might have entered your mind to say it is a dwelling; it teaches us
that it is not a dwelling. 'rather, what do you have
to say' - when you explained 'ne'otot' as 'adorn themselves'
there, then one baraita would contradict the other, and we would say it is
a Tannaitic dispute. 'and some obligate' - and this is the Tannaitic dispute; and each
one of the Amoraim resolves it according to his own reasoning: Rav
Kahana resolves that they disagree about the plain case, but
where they adorn themselves, all obligate; and Rav Yehuda
resolves that they disagree about the adorning case, but the plain case
all exempt. 'and in which the women make use' -
meaning: the hay house, the cattle house,
and the wood house, in which the women bathe; and as for the immersion
house, even though it taught us the bathhouse, it needed
to teach us the immersion house, even though it has no
filth. 'and coops' - a place where chickens are raised.
This ('house') is the catchword anticipating 11b's opening comment.
